title: Past business: enough for civil arrest?

scenes.dialogue: Advocates, a man loses a money suit. He once ran a pharma company. Is that alone enough to have him arrested in execution of the decree?
He told the court his company's turnover was forty to fifty lakh a year, but it closed in twenty twelve. The court below ordered an arrest warrant. Was that right?
scenes.shown: He told the court his company's turnover was ₹40 to 50 lakh a year, but it closed in 2012. The court below ordered an arrest warrant. Was that right?

scenes.dialogue: Hi, I'm Ravishankar from LawWorld. On thirtieth October, Honourable Justice Purushottam Kumar Chintalapudi of the Andhra Pradesh High Court ruled.
scenes.shown: Hi, I'm Ravishankar from LawWorld. On 30 October, Honourable Justice Purushottam Kumar Chintalapudi of the Andhra Pradesh High Court ruled.

scenes.dialogue: The decree-holder won a money decree in twenty seventeen. He sought the judgment-debtor's arrest, under Order Twenty One, Rules Thirty Seven and Thirty Eight.
scenes.shown: The decree-holder won a money decree in 2017. He sought the judgment-debtor's arrest, under Order XXI, Rules 37 and 38.

scenes.dialogue: He said the judgment-debtor runs a business, has gold and cash, and is wilfully avoiding payment. The judgment-debtor denied it, citing heavy losses.
At the enquiry, neither side produced documents. Citing his evidence of the company's turnover and his income tax status, the court below found he could pay.
In revision, the judgment-debtor said past business is not present means. The decree-holder replied that the court-ordered quarter deposit showed he could pay.

scenes.dialogue: Finally, what did the High Court decide? The decree-holder must prove means and wilful refusal. Past business, or his parents' land, does not by itself prove his means.
The arrest order was set aside, and the case remanded. The decree-holder may withdraw the deposit, and the judgment-debtor must pay the balance in two phases.
